lead: A MOSFET that is off still passes a small current. Below threshold the surface is weakly inverted, not empty, so drain current falls exponentially with gate voltage instead of dropping to zero. This subthreshold current, plus gate-oxide tunnelling and junction leakage, sets much of a chip's standby power. Designers quote the off current I<sub>off</sub> per micrometre of width and use the subthreshold swing to compare processes. It decides how low the supply voltage can go before standby power becomes unacceptable.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.2 for threshold voltage and its temperature trend, and Chapter 1.3 for the above-threshold current this curve joins.

blocks.text: When V<sub>GS</sub> is below V<sub>th</sub>, the gate has not formed a strong inversion layer. A small inversion charge still exists. The channel is weakly inverted, and drain current is limited by diffusion of carriers over the source barrier rather than by drift along the channel. That is why current depends exponentially on gate voltage.
I<sub>D</sub> ≈ µ C<sub>ox</sub> (W/L)(n − 1) V<sub>T</sub><sup>2</sup> e<sup>(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>th</sub>)/(nV<sub>T</sub>)</sup> (1 − e<sup>−V<sub>DS</sub>/V<sub>T</sub></sup>)
blocks.where: I<sub>D</sub> is drain current in A; µ is carrier mobility in m²/(V·s); C<sub>ox</sub> is gate oxide capacitance per unit area in F/m²; W and L are channel width and length in m; n = 1 + C<sub>d</sub>/C<sub>ox</sub> is the body factor, with C<sub>d</sub> the depletion capacitance per unit area; V<sub>T</sub> = kT/q is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at 300 K; V<sub>th</sub> is threshold voltage; V<sub>GS</sub> and V<sub>DS</sub> are gate-source and drain-source voltages. The exponent uses the thermal V<sub>T</sub>, never V<sub>th</sub>. n is between 1.0 and 1.5 for a bulk device.

blocks.text: For V<sub>DS</sub> greater than about 3V<sub>T</sub>, the last bracket is close to 1. The curve is then a straight line on a log-current against V<sub>GS</sub> graph. The exponential law holds for V<sub>GS</sub> a few tenths of a volt below V<sub>th</sub>. Above V<sub>th</sub> the square law of Chapter 1.3 takes over. In the narrow moderate-inversion band around V<sub>th</sub> neither formula is exact, so the real curve bends smoothly from exponential to square law instead of meeting at a point. A lower V<sub>th</sub> shifts the line left and raises current at every gate voltage below threshold.
The inverse of that line's slope, expressed as a gate voltage, is the subthreshold swing S. It is the gate voltage needed to change I<sub>D</sub> by one decade, a factor of 10:

blocks.where: S is in mV/decade; 2.3 = ln 10; the other symbols are as above. Typical values are 70 to 100 mV/decade. The best possible bulk MOSFET at 300 K has n = 1 and S = 2.3 × 26 mV ≈ 60 mV/decade. Smaller S means a sharper switch.

blocks.text: Off current Ioff is quoted at VGS = 0 and VDS = VDD, normally in nA/µm of transistor width. VDD is the supply voltage. A wider transistor leaks proportionally more, so a per-µm number compares processes fairly. Shorter L shifts Vth through short-channel effects (Chapter 1.6) and narrower W shifts it through the narrow-width effect; both change Ioff. Temperature matters: Ioff roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise. A 25 °C value can be 64 times larger at 85 °C.

Subthreshold conduction is not the only leak. Direct gate-oxide tunnelling flows from gate to channel when the oxide is thin. It becomes serious below about 2 nm of silicon dioxide, because electrons tunnel through the barrier. High-k dielectrics reduce this for a given capacitance.

Gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL) appears at low V<sub>GS</sub> and high V<sub>DS</sub>. The gate overlaps the drain; the field there bends the drain band so much that electrons tunnel from valence to conduction band. Tunnelled electrons are collected by the drain and the holes go to the body, so the conventional GIDL current flows from the drain to the body. Either way, the drain terminal carries this extra current even when the channel is off.

A reverse-biased source-body or drain-body junction also leaks. Thermal generation in the depletion region adds a small current. In modern processes these paths together can equal or exceed subthreshold current. Each has a different bias dependence, so one I<sub>off</sub> number hides which path dominates. See Unit 3 for the power budget and Unit 6 for leakage test structures.

figure.caption: The plot shows log drain current against gate voltage. Both curves pass through 0.4 V and 10<sup>−7</sup> A; the steeper curve reaches a given low current at a smaller gate voltage.

spec.aria: Two straight-line subthreshold plots of log drain current against gate voltage, the steeper 60 mV per decade line reaching a given current at a much lower gate voltage.

examples.question: A process has subthreshold swing S = 80 mV/decade and I<sub>off</sub> = 10 nA/µm at V<sub>th</sub> = 0.3 V. A designer raises V<sub>th</sub> by 100 mV. (a) Find the leakage reduction factor. (b) Find the new I<sub>off</sub>. (c) A chip has 10 mm of total transistor width. Find its new total leakage and compare with the original. (d) Find n. Take V<sub>T</sub> = 26 mV.
steps: 1. S = 80 mV/decade means every 80 mV rise in V<sub>th</sub> cuts I<sub>off</sub> by 10×. For ΔV<sub>th</sub> = 100 mV, factor = 10<sup>100/80</sup> = 10<sup>1.25</sup> = 17.78.
3. Total width W = 10 mm = 10 000 µm. New total = 0.562 nA/µm × 10 000 µm = 5 623 nA = 5.62 µA. Original = 10 nA/µm × 10 000 µm = 100 000 nA = 100 µA.
examples.answer: The factor is 17.78, I<sub>off</sub> falls to 0.56 nA/µm, the chip leaks 5.62 µA instead of 100 µA, and n = 1.34.
examples.check:
import math
S = 80.0
dVth = 100.0
Ioff = 10.0
W_um = 10000.0
factor = 10**(dVth/S)
Ioff_new = Ioff/factor
total_new_uA = Ioff_new*W_um/1000.0
VT = 0.026
n = (S/1000.0)/(2.3*VT)
print(round(factor, 2))
print(round(Ioff_new, 2))
print(round(total_new_uA, 2))
print(round(n, 2))

traps: Using V<sub>T</sub> for both threshold and thermal voltage. The exponent uses V<sub>T</sub> = kT/q ≈ 26 mV; the threshold is V<sub>th</sub> (or V<sub>T0</sub>).
Claiming a bulk MOSFET can have S below 60 mV/decade at room temperature. S = 2.3nV<sub>T</sub> with n ≥ 1 sets a floor near 60 mV/decade.
Treating I<sub>off</sub> as a fixed current. It is quoted per µm of width, so total leakage changes with total W and with L through V<sub>th</sub>.
Saying the transistor carries no current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0. I<sub>off</sub> is defined at exactly that bias, with V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>.
Forgetting the direction of temperature dependence. Leakage rises with temperature, roughly doubling every 10 °C, not falling.

quiz.q: Define subthreshold swing S. Give a typical value and the room-temperature floor.
quiz.a: S is the gate voltage for one decade change in I<sub>D</sub>; typical 70–100 mV/decade, floor about 60 mV/decade at 300 K.

quiz.q: Why is 60 mV/decade a floor for a bulk MOSFET at 300 K?
quiz.a: S = 2.3nV<sub>T</sub>, n ≥ 1, and V<sub>T</sub> ≈ 26 mV; minimum S = 2.3 × 26 mV ≈ 60 mV/decade.

quiz.q: S = 90 mV/decade. V<sub>th</sub> rises by 45 mV. By what factor does I<sub>off</sub> fall?
A bulk planar MOSFET at 300 K is measured with S = 55 mV/decade. What is the likely explanation?
quiz.a: Impossible for bulk at 300 K because the floor is about 60 mV/decade; likely measurement error, not a bulk device, or a different temperature.

quiz.q: Why is I<sub>off</sub> quoted per µm of width?
quiz.a: Total leakage scales with width; a per-µm number allows comparison across different transistor sizes.

quiz.q: I<sub>off</sub> doubles every 10 °C. By what factor does it grow from 25 °C to 85 °C?
At V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 a datasheet gives I<sub>off</sub> = 1 nA/µm. Does that mean the transistor is off? Explain.
quiz.a: No. It is weakly off but still leaks. I<sub>off</sub> is the specified off-state current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 and V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>, per µm.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, subthreshold swing and I<sub>off</sub> are first-line numbers in a process design kit; search for these terms with GIDL and high-k/metal gate. FinFETs and gate-all-around devices improve control so S stays near the floor and short-channel V<sub>th</sub> shifts shrink. Tunnel FETs try to beat the 60 mV/decade limit by changing the injection mechanism, but they are research devices. See Unit 3 for power budgeting and Unit 6 for measurements on test structures.
